peopleAlsoAsk.question: What is the difference between emulsion and Pickering emulsion?
peopleAlsoAsk.snippet: Solid Particles. The most notable difference between a Pickering emulsion and a classical emulsion is that, the former one bears solid particles on the interface between two liquid phases serving as the stabilizing agent, whereas the latter uses molecular surfactants to stabilize emulsions.

peopleAlsoAsk.question: What is the stabilizer for Pickering emulsions?
peopleAlsoAsk.snippet: Solid particles commonly used to stabilize Pickering emulsions are: food-grade organic materials such as polysaccharide particles, protein particles, lipid particles, and safe inorganic particles such as silica, calcium carbonate, and hydroxyapatite (Hap) [3].

peopleAlsoAsk.question: How to stabilize a water-in-oil emulsion?
peopleAlsoAsk.snippet: One of the easiest ways to improve stability is to increase the dispersed water phase to >60%. This increases the viscosity of the emulsion due to internal phase packing. Using the correct emulsifier and level is also critical.
peopleAlsoAsk.title: Ask the Expert: My water-in-oil emulsion is unstable. What can I do?

peopleAlsoAsk.question: What is the Pickering emulsion method?
peopleAlsoAsk.snippet: The Pickering emulsion method refers to the stabilization of oil/water emulsions by using solid particles, such as viral particles, that segregate at the liquid/liquid interface, enhancing the stability of the droplets formed within the emulsion.
